The game feels like a "everything and the kitchen sink" of RPG systems, and it's fun, but it also makes it inconsistent. some actions you'll only ever preform once, and a lot of them lack polish. The standout example is the "Outlaw" capture. There are a dozen ways to travel, but if you're turning in an outlaw, you have to walk to the nearest prison dropoff. Sometimes this means riding horseback clear to the other end of the huge map, and if anything goes wrong, it will hard lock the turn in. In my case, the guard got distracted by something, left his post, and I couldn't turn in my bounty, even after waiting a good long while.

Crimson Desert will not hold your hand, even when you really wish it would. Some puzzles and mechanics are so obtuse, you really have no choice but to look up a guide and hope someone else has figured it out.

The story is terrible. I didn't play before "Enhanced", but the updated story leaves much to be desired even after the improvements.

Also, Yann sucks.

The worst thing however is the game either crashing or not running at all. On first launch, I had to fight with the game to even start. Then today, after 150+ hours, the game won't even launch or load. IT troubleshooting sours a game very quickly.

If you enjoy exploring vast, open worlds that don’t hand-hold you through every mystery, this game is something special. It rewards curiosity and lets you uncover its secrets at your own pace, which makes every discovery feel genuinely earned.

The combat is fast, fluid, and combo-driven, offering plenty of depth once you get comfortable with the controls. On top of that, there’s a satisfying mix of puzzles that break up the action nicely.

What really sets it apart is the sheer variety of things you can do. You can cook, craft, set up your own campsite, go fishing, mining, and more—it almost feels like a single-player MMO with how much content and freedom it offers.

Visually, the game is stunning, with a world that constantly invites you to wander just a little further. It has that rare “wanderlust” quality where the journey itself is just as rewarding as any objective.

It might take a bit of time to fully click, but once it does, it becomes a truly unique and memorable experience.
It's a huge game filled with everything, but if you value your own time you'll continually ask yourself what the point of it all is.

I put 64 hours into this, messed with endless settings and keybinds, and finally realized I was only still playing because I spent money on it.

The game looks amazing, but it’s an absolute chore. It feels like an MMO crammed into a single-player game—drowning in useless junk loot, cluttered menus, and upgrades that barely make a difference. The open world has no real challenge; regular enemies fall over in seconds, so only the big bosses are actually fun to fight.

Everything outside the basic combat feels unfinished. Stealth is completely broken (guards are either blind or instantly spot you from miles away), and the puzzles are obscure and annoying.

If you just run around suplexing enemies and ignore 80% of the game's extra systems, you might have some fun. Otherwise, it feels less like an adventure and more like a second job.

It's a great game, for BDO players like me.
They improved most aspects of their previous mmo and wrapped it in the new shell of single player game. Combat is simplified yet clean and precise, if you know what you are doing, fighting hordes can be Dynasty Warrior and bosses can be DMC.
Lifeskilling got streamlined and became easier without farming 100 hrs to get basic materials then combine 50 of them to create same material lv2. You can still afk to profit if you want tho.
Graphics is insane due to the draw distance, no game even comes close to this level of LOD. But the optimization is not the best around. Yes it can run 4k, yes it can run RT, yet the game is an absolute hot mess without RR, which even on 5080 is a 20 fps situation. I'm not bothered by the pop-ins at all, since I know they improved it compared to BDO vastly.
In conclusion, CD is a game where you can do anything you can think of, just don't think too deep.

Great game, story, flow, etc. But still has a road ahead on optimization. This game has undoubtedly the most options for graphics, and while my hardware isn't rare - I'd say the pixel count may be less common. With LG's 45 inch GX9, I am lucky enough to witness 5K in all its fine detail, but with Crimson Desert in its current state of optimization I cannot run full resolution and graphic settings without substantial frame rate issues. I understand it sits under a huge umbrella of CPU scheduling, draw calls, asset streaming, share compilation, VRAM residency, frame pacing, specific ray tracing implementation, location effects, and list goes on to compile a weak above-4K optimization. I know, first world problems, but I think it's still important to point out. As tech advances, my specific setup becomes more common, available, and affordable. With such an ambitious title as Crimson Desert - it is still important to point out that at this time: Crimson Desert does terribly with 5K even if you're running highest end consumer-level gear. For others, I recommend this game. For those in the same boat as I am: I do not recommend it at this time.
